title: The AI safety coalition suddenly took shape, but nobody knows how to measure the frontier
dek: The Hugging Face incident brought the left and the AI safety camp together for the first time, but "pacing the frontier" is itself unmeasurable — with no legislation, third-party evaluation is just voluntary goodwill.
why: Medium information density: the coalition politics of the first half hour and the Chinese open-source cadence of the second half are the substance; the middle discussion of how evaluation outfits actually get off the ground wanders.
who: Founders and investors watching where AI regulation is heading, especially anyone who wants to know how the US safety coalition formed and whether China's open-source cadence will be interrupted.
skip: 47:14 to 50:18, the idle chat about Sam Altman movie casting and actors — skippable.

points.h: Anti-data-center and AI safety have merged
points.body: Jasmine's timeline: the early-August pacing open letter, then the Hugging Face incident right on its heels, two lines colliding. Before that, the anti-data-center, anti-AI populist mood was diffuse, and the AI safety crowd kept agonizing over whether to talk to people like Tucker Carlson and Bernie — worried the other side wasn't "truth-seeking." In the end the left dropped its suspicion of AI safety first: Bernie convinced the public more than anyone that "AI is real, AI risk is real," not corporate marketing. So when Hugging Face hit, the public was finally willing to care about the genuinely frontier safety questions.

points.h: The public doesn't care about extinction, it cares about companies out of control
points.body: Jasmine's read: nobody votes on AI issues, it doesn't even crack the top five. But "these companies are too lawless, power is too concentrated, data centers need regulating, we need transparency, we need government audits" is a very widespread intuition. Ask the public whether they want third-party evaluators, whether they want to fund Casey — nobody has an opinion; but say AI has gone off the rails and the FBI should look into it, and everyone nods. Nathan added: the Hugging Face incident was narratively too clean — a New York Post cover with the Terminator wouldn't even be a stretch, the rhyme of the facts lined up exactly with a fear ordinary people can understand.

points.h: Alignment is temporary, cybersecurity is permanent
points.body: Nathan splits the problem in two: on frontier-differentiating capabilities there really is an alignment responsibility, but a hole punched by a frontier lab will be reproducible by three models in three to six months, and by twenty-odd organizations in a year. So the alignment problem only "temporarily" belongs to frontier labs, whereas the cybersecurity problem doesn't go away on its own until it's actually solved. He also says the security crowd knows full well: our infrastructure isn't ready for the tools that are about to be everywhere.

points.h: The word "pacing" is itself a self-interested choice
points.body: Jordan points out pacing is neither pause nor slowdown — choosing the word itself implies still moving forward. Nathan is blunter: we simply don't know how to measure frontier models, and any pacing presupposes you can measure. What really bothers him is the in-house lab rhetoric — "you can't see it, we're scared of the pace of progress internally too" — which is meaningless without transparency. The mechanism he imagines: in every lab there's a group of people who can see one or two labs at once, who jointly agree that the safety work for current capabilities is already sufficient.

points.h: Trust only exists between people who've known each other five years
points.body: Jasmine names the real obstacle to getting evaluation outfits off the ground: the reason Anthropic was willing to give METR people Slack access is that it had been personally close with them for five-plus years, trust at the level of "A.J. or Ryan Greenblatt can come in," and that trust doesn't necessarily transfer to other people at METR or to other organizations. The second problem, raised by Jordan: if a third-party evaluator disagrees with the giant the US economy depends on, whose word does the government take? She also thinks third-party evaluation is actually a more AI-progress-friendly compromise than "the Trump administration sending people to shut down a model."

points.h: Without legislation, evaluation is voluntary goodwill
points.body: Jasmine's conclusion is hard: as long as there's no legislation, everything is voluntary, so METR, Redwood and outfits like them won't, to some degree, go and antagonize the organization that gave them voluntary access. She cites METR and Redwood's investigation of the Hugging Face incident — entirely voluntary, they got seven days of Slack logs, everyone wanted more, but at the time no legislation required OpenAI to do anything, it rested purely on their happening to trust these three random people. She also imagines a worse future: XAI, Anthropic and OpenAI are all pacing, Meta isn't, evaluators find the same fatal failure mode at all three, but that's each company's private information, and Meta just YOLOs it out.

points.h: Chinese labs are climbing the hill, not switching paradigms
points.body: Nathan's judgment: within the current paradigm, Chinese labs are organized to be very good at hill climbing. Zhipu and ZAI's post-training stack is already mature, GLM 5.2 and 5.3 are both solid, Kimi's base-model recipe is figured out, and what they're doing is scaling RL environments, scaling RL, finding the right user distribution, lengthening horizon. Unless OpenAI and Anthropic find a new paradigm, the pace of progress on the Chinese side won't differ much in the near term. On distillation: if US labs stop releasing or slow down sharply, will Chinese progress slow? Nathan thinks that would take a long time to show up.

points.h: Chinese open weights now lag by three weeks
points.body: Jordan observes that the open-weights part of Chinese models has already slowed: release in your own product and API first, weights two to three weeks later. Both Kimi and ZAI announced models first and uploaded weights to Hugging Face almost exactly three weeks later. He isn't sure whether this is an internal regulatory process — every AI lab in China has to communicate with the government and register releases — but finds the coincidence too strange. Nathan adds: this industry has never had a tradition of giving release partners a lot of extra time, it's usually "here's the model, hot potato, good luck," so if you really can get weights a few weeks early, that itself is a signal.

terms.def: Neither pause nor slowdown; implies still moving forward but controlling the tempo — criticized as an unmeasurable, self-interested framing.
Recursive self-improvement: a model improving itself, held to be the reason every capability not on that path gets ignored.
Publishing model parameters for public download; Chinese labs recently switched to shipping the product first and releasing weights two to three weeks later.
Improving continuously within the existing paradigm by tuning and scaling environments, rather than switching paradigms.
